name: Maya Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Maya, I'm 27. I'm a junior buyer at Harlow and Sons, a family-run firm that supplies cleaning products to schools, offices and care homes: bleach, mop heads, bin bags, hand soap, paper towels. I still live with my parents, which is how I've saved so much. I'm engaged to Imran, who's a driving instructor, and we're getting married next summer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I go through the stock sheets in the morning, on paper, because I like to tick things off with a pen. Then I phone our suppliers, the same ones the firm has used for twenty years, and place the orders. My boss Mr Harlow, the founder's son, checks my work and corrects my maths more often than I'd like. I enjoy the care homes, they're always grateful. I don't enjoy the computer system, which I only use because I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always get talked up. At work I'd say good, now we can get on with it. I wouldn't post about it, I'm not online much except for family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I've never used one of these AI tools and I never wanted to. Mr Harlow runs the firm the old way, and in this picture that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, learn the products properly, and keep saving for the wedding and a house. Between my savings and Imran's we've got well over a year of our pay. I'd maybe ask Mr Harlow to teach me how he negotiates with suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in this world a worry for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the firm lost contracts. A big company in the city has been undercutting Harlow and Sons on school contracts, and we lost two last year. That's the real worry here, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the next few years look like for you, in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house near my parents, children, and me still at Harlow and Sons, maybe part time once we have kids. That's the plan.

I'd say at work **good**, now we can get on with it.
think: I'd be **relieved**, since I've never used AI tools and never wanted to.
Mr Harlow runs the firm **the old way**, and that's fine here.
do: Learn the **products** properly and ask Mr Harlow how he **negotiates**.
Keep saving with Imran for the **wedding and a house**.
S0.quote: A big company in the city has been undercutting Harlow and Sons on school contracts, and we lost two last year.
fieldNote: Her worry is a **bigger rival** undercutting school contracts, not AI.
Living at home and an **engagement** give her strong savings and clear plans.
She trusts the **family firm** and its old ways.

steps.text: Ask Mr Harlow to teach her supplier negotiation
Keep saving with Imran for the wedding and a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be careful about handing everything to computers. At work I'd say Harlow and Sons has always been about people knowing people. I'd say it at the mosque too, to the older ladies, and they'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it worries me a bit, but My boss Mr Harlow has always said Harlow and Sons will never replace a loyal worker with a machine. I believe him. If the big city firms use AI and we don't, we might lose more contracts, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well. I'd ask Mr Harlow what he plans to do. I wouldn't sign up for any computer course unless he asked me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I trust him, but things are moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mr Harlow decided he had to bring the AI in to compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn, I suppose, because he's the boss. But I'd hate it, and I'd be slow. I'd ask my cousin Bilal, he's good with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the firm loses contracts to the big companies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the firm might shrink, and that's a real risk. But the care homes like dealing with a person they know, and I don't think that changes quickly.

I'd say Harlow and Sons has always been about **people knowing people**.

Ask Mr Harlow directly what he **plans** to do.
Avoid any **computer course** unless he asks.

S1.quote: My boss Mr Harlow has always said Harlow and Sons will never replace a loyal worker with a machine.
fieldNote: She expects to **keep her job** through the owner's loyalty.
She sees the real risk as the firm **losing contracts** to AI-using rivals.
She'd only learn the tools if **her boss asked**, with her cousin's help.

steps.text: Ask Mr Harlow what he plans to do about AI
Keep doing the daily stock sheets and supplier calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and families will pay the price. I'd say at the mosque that we need to look after each other. I'd tell my friends to hold on to their savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Harlow and Sons couldn't hold out. If AI can do all thinking work by 2028, the big firms will sell to schools so cheaply that Mr Harlow has to change or close. I'd be the first one to go, because I'm the junior and I can barely use the computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on buying a house, and we'd have a smaller wedding. Imran and I would keep every penny saved. I'd look for something hands-on, maybe at my aunt's bakery, because that has a few years till the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Imran's work as a driving instructor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His job is hands-on, but self-driving cars come with the robots, don't they? So his lasts till about 2031, maybe. That's three years of his income and our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family. My parents would help, and Imran's family too. That's what family is for. I wouldn't want government money if I could avoid it.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and families will pay the price.
I'd tell friends at the mosque to **look after each other** and keep savings.
think: Harlow and Sons couldn't hold out; Mr Harlow would **change or close**.
As the junior who can barely use the computer, I'd **go first**.
do: Hold off on the **house** and have a **smaller wedding**.
Look for hands-on work at my aunt's **bakery**.
S2.quote: I'd be the first one to go, because I'm the junior and I can barely use the computer.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** quickly, even at a loyal family firm.
Imran's driving job buys about **three years** before robots and self-driving cars.
She'd lean on **family**, not government, in keeping with her views.

steps.text: Postpone the house purchase with Imran
Cut the wedding guest list and budget
Ask her aunt for work at the family bakery
Lean on both families for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, so families should prepare. I'd say to my friends: save, don't borrow. At work I'd say we should talk to Mr Harlow about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job goes around 2031, I think. But with five years, we could get married and get settled before it hits. Maybe I'd be having children by then and stepping back anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned, and buy a small house in 2027. I'd stay at Harlow and Sons as long as they'll have me. I might learn baking properly from my aunt at weekends, so I have something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's time. I can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Imran in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Imran's lessons would last till about 2034 with the robots later. My fiancé Imran says people will want a human driving instructor for years after the cars can drive themselves. I hope he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to work after children, if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, if I had to. If my job goes and Imran's lasts a few years, we can manage on one wage. My mother did it.

say: I'd tell my friends that families should **prepare**: save, and **don't borrow**.
I'd suggest at work that we talk to Mr Harlow about **the future** of the firm.
think: My job goes around **2031**, but we can settle first.
I might be having **children** and stepping back by then anyway.
do: Have the **wedding** as planned and buy a **small house** in 2027.
Learn **baking** from my aunt at weekends, so I have hands-on skills.
feel: **Anxious**, but there's time to **plan** around it.
S3.quote: My fiancé Imran says people will want a human driving instructor for years after the cars can drive themselves.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose the job**, but times family plans around it.
She'd manage on **one wage**, like her mother did.
She hopes, without certainty, that people want a **human instructor**.

steps.text: Buy a small house with Imran in 2027

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and we should use it to look after our families and communities. I'd say we don't need to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2036 I hope to have children and be at home with them, at least part time. Imran's work lasts until the robots around 2039. So for us it's later, but I'd still worry about the children's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. Wedding, house, children, as we planned. Keep saving. Maybe Imran would think about running his own small driving school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far off, but I think about the children I don't have yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you worry about for the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What jobs they'd do. If computers do all the thinking and robots do the hands-on work, I don't know what I'd tell my children to study. That's the bit that keeps coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach them, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good values and hard work. And maybe a trade. And faith. Whatever else changes, they'll need those.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long, so we should look after families and **communities**.
I'd say we **don't need to panic**.
think: By 2036 I hope to be **at home** with children, at least part time.
Imran's work lasts until **2039**, but the children's future worries me.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding, house and children** as planned.
Encourage Imran to consider his own **driving school**.
feel: **Uneasy**; far off, but she thinks of the **children** she doesn't have yet.
S4.quote: I don't know what I'd tell my children to study.
fieldNote: Her own income matters less because she plans to **stay home** with children.
Her worry shifts to **her children's** future and what they should study.

steps.text: Go ahead with the wedding, house and children as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job would go, the firm might close, and Imran's work only lasts a few years after that. What would help is apprenticeships for people like me, paid by employers, and businesses like Harlow and Sons getting a fair chance against the big firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. Whatever the computers do, my mother says God gave people hands and a mind for a reason, and I hold on to that.

headlineQuote: Whatever the computers do, my mother says God gave people hands and a mind for a reason, and I hold on to that.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old** junior buyer at Harlow and Sons, a family cleaning supplies firm.
She lives with her parents, is **engaged** to Imran, a driving instructor, and has strong savings.
She has never used AI and trusts her boss's **loyalty** in milder scenarios.
In fast scenarios she'd **postpone the house**, cut the wedding and lean on family.
Her deepest worry is **her future children**: what they should study and do.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job and the firm could go, with Imran's soon after.
whatWouldHelp: **Employer-paid apprenticeships** and a fair chance for **small firms** against big ones.
